blocks.p: Then the porter, Mr. Watchful, asked Christiana about her country and her family.
“I came from the City of Destruction,” she said. “I am a widow; my husband is dead. His name was Christian, the pilgrim.”
“What!” said the porter. “Was he your husband?”
“Yes,” she said, “and these are his children; and this,” pointing to Mercy, “is a neighbor from my town.”

Then the porter rang his bell, as he does at such times, and one of the young women of the house came to the door, whose name was Humble-mind. “Go and tell them inside,” the porter said to her, “that Christiana, the wife of Christian, and her children have come here on pilgrimage.” So she went in and told them. And what a noise of gladness there was inside the moment that word was out of her mouth! They came hurrying to the porter, for Christiana was still standing at the door. Then some of the most senior of them said to her, “Come in, Christiana, come in, wife of that good man; come in, blessed woman; come in, with all who are with you.” So she went in, and her children and her companion followed her. Once inside, they were led into a very large room and asked to sit down, and the heads of the house were called to see and welcome the guests. They came in, and when they understood who the visitors were, they greeted each of them with a kiss and said, “Welcome, vessels of the grace of God; welcome to us, your friends.”

Because it was now rather late, and because the pilgrims were weary from their journey and still faint from the sight of the fight and of the terrible lions, they wanted to get ready for bed as soon as they could. “No,” said the family, “refresh yourselves first with a bite to eat.” For they had prepared a lamb for them, with the sauce that always goes with it [Exod. 12:21, 28; John 1:29], because the porter had heard of their coming beforehand and had told those inside. So when they had eaten, and ended their prayers with a psalm, they asked if they might go to rest.

“If we may be so bold as to choose,” said Christiana, “let us sleep in the room that was my husband’s when he was here.” So they took them up to it, and they all lay in one room. When they had settled, Christiana and Mercy fell to talking about fitting things.
“I little thought once,” said Christiana, “when my husband set out on pilgrimage, that I would ever follow him.”
“And you thought even less of lying in his bed, in his room, to rest, as you are now.”
“And less still of seeing his face with comfort, and of worshiping the Lord the King together with him. Yet now I believe I shall.”
“Listen! Don’t you hear a noise?”
“Yes. I believe it is music, for joy that we are here.”
“Wonderful!” said Mercy. “Music in the house, music in the heart, and music in heaven too, for joy that we are here!”

So they talked a while, and then went to sleep. In the morning, when they were awake, Christiana said to Mercy, “What was the matter with you, laughing in your sleep last night? I suppose you were dreaming.”
“So I was, and a sweet dream it was. But are you sure I laughed?”
“Yes, you laughed heartily. Come, Mercy, tell me your dream.”

“I dreamed that I sat all alone in a lonely place, grieving over the hardness of my heart. I had not sat there long before it seemed to me that a crowd gathered around me, to look at me and hear what I was saying. So they listened, and I went on grieving over the hardness of my heart. At this some of them laughed at me, some called me a fool, and some began to shove me about. Then I looked up, and saw someone with wings coming toward me. He came straight to me and said, ‘Mercy, what is troubling you?’ And when he had heard my complaint, he said, ‘Peace be to you.’ He wiped my eyes with his handkerchief, and dressed me in silver and gold. He put a chain around my neck, and earrings in my ears, and a beautiful crown on my head. [Ezek. 16:8-12] Then he took me by the hand and said, ‘Mercy, come after me.’ So he went up, and I followed him, until we came to a golden gate. He knocked; and when those inside had opened it, the man went in, and I followed him up to a throne, on which Someone sat, who said to me, ‘Welcome, daughter.’ The place looked bright and twinkling, like the stars, or rather like the sun; and I thought I saw your husband there. Then I woke from my dream. But did I laugh?”

“Laugh! Yes, and well you might, to see yourself so well off. For you must let me tell you that I believe it was a good dream; and as you have begun to find the first part of it true, so you will find the second part true at last. ‘God speaks once, yes twice, yet no one notices it: in a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls on people as they slumber on their beds.’ [Job 33:14-15] We need not lie awake in bed to talk with God. He can visit us while we sleep, and make us hear his voice then. Our heart is often awake while we sleep, and God can speak to it, by words, by proverbs, by signs and pictures, as well as if we were awake.”
“Well, I am glad of my dream,” said Mercy, “for I hope before long to see it fulfilled, and to laugh again.”
“I think it is high time we got up and found out what we are to do.”

“Please, if they invite us to stay a while, let’s accept gladly. I would like to stay here a while and get better acquainted with these young women. Prudence, Piety, and Charity seem to me to have very lovely, serious faces.”
“We will see what they do.”
So when they were up and dressed, they came down, and the others asked whether they had rested well.
“Very well,” said Mercy. “It was one of the best nights’ lodging I ever had in my life.”
Then Prudence and Piety said, “If you can be persuaded to stay here a while, you shall have whatever the house can offer.”
“Yes,” said Charity, “and with a very good will.”

So they agreed, and stayed there about a month or more, and did one another a great deal of good. And because Prudence wanted to see how Christiana had brought up her children, she asked her leave to question them on their faith. Christiana gave it freely. So Prudence began with the youngest, whose name was James.
“Come, James,” she said. “Can you tell me who made you?”
“God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.”
“Good boy. And can you tell me who saves you?”
“God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.”
“Good boy still. But how does God the Father save you?”
“By his grace.”
“How does God the Son save you?”
“By his righteousness, death, and blood, and life.”
“And how does God the Holy Spirit save you?”
“By giving me light, by making me new, and by keeping me safe.”

Then Prudence said to Christiana, “You are to be commended for bringing up your children like this. I suppose I needn’t ask the rest these questions, since the youngest can answer them so well. I will turn to the next youngest.” And she said, “Come, Joseph” (for his name was Joseph), “will you let me question you?”
“With all my heart.”
“What is man?”
“A reasoning creature, made so by God, as my brother said.”
“What is meant by the word ‘saved’?”
“That man, by sin, has brought himself into a state of captivity and misery.”
“What is meant by his being saved by the Trinity?”
“That sin is so great and mighty a tyrant that no one can pull us out of its clutches but God; and that God is so good and loving toward man that he does indeed pull him out of this miserable state.”
“What is God’s purpose in saving poor men?”
“The glory of his name, of his grace, and of his justice, and the everlasting happiness of his creature.”
“Who are the ones who will be saved?”
“Those who accept his salvation.”

“Good boy, Joseph; your mother has taught you well, and you have listened to what she said.” Then Prudence said to Samuel, the second oldest, “Come, Samuel, are you willing for me to question you too?”
“Yes, indeed, if you please.”
“What is heaven?”
“A place and a state most blessed, because God lives there.”
“What is hell?”
“A place and a state most miserable, because it is the dwelling place of sin, the devil, and death.”
“Why do you want to go to heaven?”
“So that I may see God and serve him without weariness; so that I may see Christ and love him forever; so that I may have that fullness of the Holy Spirit in me which I can by no means enjoy here.”
“A very good boy too, and one who has learned well.” Then she turned to the eldest, whose name was Matthew, and said to him, “Come, Matthew, shall I question you as well?”
“With a very good will.”
“Then I ask: was there ever anything that existed before God?”
“No; for God is eternal, and nothing but himself existed until the beginning of the first day. ‘For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them.’”
“What do you think of the Bible?”
“It is the holy Word of God.”
“Is there nothing written in it that you don’t understand?”
“Yes, a great deal.”
“What do you do when you come to passages in it that you don’t understand?”
“I think that God is wiser than I am. I also pray that he will be pleased to let me know everything in it that he knows will be for my good.”
“What do you believe about the resurrection of the dead?”

“I believe they will rise, the same that were buried: the same in nature, though not in corruption. And I believe this for two reasons: first, because God has promised it; second, because he is able to do it.”

Then Prudence said to the boys, “You must keep on listening to your mother, for she can teach you more. You must also listen carefully to the good talk you hear from others, for it is for your sakes that they say good things. Notice too, and carefully, what the heavens and the earth teach you; but above all, spend much time meditating on that Book that made your father become a pilgrim. For my part, my children, I will teach you what I can while you are here, and I will be glad if you ask me questions that build you up in godliness.”

Now, when these pilgrims had been in this place about a week, Mercy had a visitor who professed some goodwill toward her, and his name was Mr. Brisk, a man of some breeding who made a show of religion but clung very closely to the world. He came once or twice, or more, to Mercy, and offered her his love. Now Mercy had a fair face, and so was the more attractive. Her mind was also set on always keeping herself busy; for when she had nothing to do for herself, she would make stockings and clothing for others and give them to those in need. And Mr. Brisk, not knowing where or how she disposed of what she made, seemed greatly taken with her, because he found her never idle. “I’ll warrant she would make a good housewife,” he said to himself.

Mercy then told the young women of the house about the matter, and asked them about him, for they knew him better than she did. They told her that he was a very busy young man who made a show of religion but was, they feared, a stranger to the power of what is good. “Then I will look at him no more,” said Mercy, “for I intend never to have a drag on my soul.”

Prudence replied that there was no need to go to much trouble to discourage him: if she kept on as she had begun, working for the poor, that would quickly cool his ardor. So the next time he came, he found her at her old work, making things for the poor.
“What!” he said. “Always at it?”
“Yes,” she said, “either for myself or for others.”
“And how much can you earn in a day?”
“I do these things,” she said, “’so that I may be rich in good works, laying up a good foundation for the time to come, so that I may take hold of eternal life.’” [1 Tim. 6:17-19]
“Why, tell me, what do you do with them?”
“Clothe the naked,” she said.
At that his face fell. So he stopped coming to see her; and when he was asked the reason, he said that Mercy was a pretty girl, but burdened with bad habits.

When he had left her, Prudence said, “Didn’t I tell you that Mr. Brisk would soon abandon you? Yes, and he will spread a bad report of you too; for in spite of his show of religion and his apparent love for you, Mercy, he and you are of such different temperaments that I believe you will never come together.”

“I might have had husbands before now,” said Mercy, “though I never spoke of it to anyone; but they were men who did not like my ways, though none of them ever found fault with my person. So they and I could not agree.”
“Mercy in our day is little valued, except as a name. The practice of it, which your way of life shows, there are few who can put up with.”

“Well,” said Mercy, “if nobody will have me, I will die unmarried, or my ways shall be my husband. For I cannot change my nature, and I intend never, as long as I live, to take a man who sets himself against me in this. I had a sister named Bountiful who was married to one of these misers, and he and she could never agree. Because my sister was determined to go on as she had begun, that is, to show kindness to the poor, her husband first denounced her publicly and then turned her out of his doors.”
“And yet he professed to be a Christian, I’ll warrant you.”
“Yes, such a one as he was; and the world is full of such men now. But I want none of them.”

Now Matthew, Christiana’s eldest son, fell sick, and his sickness was severe. He had great pain in his bowels, so that at times he was doubled up with it, pulled, as it were, both ends together. Not far away there lived a Mr. Skill, an experienced and well-respected physician. So at Christiana’s request they sent for him, and he came. When he had entered the room and observed the boy a little, he concluded that he was sick with the gripes. Then he said to the mother, “What has Matthew been eating lately?”
“Nothing but what is wholesome,” said Christiana.

“This boy has been tampering with something that is lying undigested in his stomach,” the physician answered, “and it will not come away without treatment. I tell you, he must be purged, or he will die.”

“Mother, Mother,” said Samuel, “what was it my brother gathered up and ate as soon as we had come away from the gate at the head of this road? You know there was an orchard on the left, on the other side of the wall, and some of the trees hung over the wall, and my brother pulled down the fruit and ate it.”
“True, my child,” said Christiana, “he did take some and eat it. Naughty boy that he was, I scolded him, and still he would eat it.”

“I knew he had eaten something that was not wholesome food,” said Mr. Skill, “and that food, that fruit, is the most harmful of all. It is the fruit of Beelzebub’s orchard. I am amazed that no one warned you about it; many have died of it.”
Then Christiana began to cry. “Oh, naughty boy!” she said. “And oh, careless mother! What shall I do for my son?”
“Come, don’t be too downcast. The boy may yet do well; but he must purge and vomit.”
“Please, sir, try the utmost of your skill on him, whatever it costs.”

“No, I hope I shall be reasonable.” So he made him a purge, but it was too weak; it was said to be made of the blood of a goat, the ashes of a heifer, and some juice of hyssop. [Heb. 10:1-4] When Mr. Skill saw that this purge was too weak, he made him one that would do the work. It was made ex carne et sanguine Christi, from the flesh and blood of Christ [John 6:54-57; Heb. 9:14] (you know physicians give their patients strange medicines), and it was made up into pills, with a promise or two, and a suitable amount of salt. [Mark 9:49] He was to take three at a time, fasting, in half a quarter-pint of the tears of repentance.
When this medicine was prepared and brought to the boy, he was reluctant to take it, though the gripes were tearing him as if he would be pulled to pieces.
“Come, come,” said the physician, “you must take it.”
“It goes against my stomach,” said the boy. [Zech. 12:10]
“I must have you take it,” said his mother.
“I’ll only vomit it up again,” said the boy.
“Please, sir,” Christiana said to Mr. Skill, “how does it taste?”
“It has no bad taste,” said the doctor; and with that she touched one of the pills with the tip of her tongue.
“Oh, Matthew,” she said, “this medicine is sweeter than honey. If you love your mother, if you love your brothers, if you love Mercy, if you love your life, take it.”

So, with much ado, after a short prayer for God’s blessing on it, he took it, and it worked kindly in him. It made him purge; it made him sleep and rest quietly; it put him into a fine warmth and a healthy sweat, and rid him of his gripes altogether. In a little while he got up and walked about with a staff, and would go from room to room talking with Prudence, Piety, and Charity about his illness and how he was healed.
When the boy was well, Christiana asked Mr. Skill, “Sir, what will satisfy you for your trouble and care for my child?”
“You must pay the Master of the College of Physicians,” he said, “according to the rules made and provided for such cases.” [Heb. 13:11-16]
“But, sir,” she said, “what else is this pill good for?”
“It is a universal pill. It is good against every disease that pilgrims are liable to, and when it is well prepared it keeps good beyond memory.”
“Please, sir, make me up twelve boxes of them; for if I can get these, I will never take any other medicine.”

“These pills are good for preventing disease as well as for curing it when one is sick. Yes, I dare say it, and stand by it: if a man will only use this medicine as he should, it will make him live forever. [John 6:50] But, good Christiana, you must give these pills no other way than as I have prescribed; if you do, they will do no good.” So he gave Christiana medicine for herself and her boys and for Mercy, told Matthew to be careful how he ate any more green plums, kissed them, and went his way.
You were told before that Prudence had invited the boys to ask her, whenever they liked, questions that might do them good, and that she would say something in reply.
Then Matthew, who had been sick, asked her, “Why, for the most part, is medicine bitter to our taste?”
“To show how unwelcome the Word of God, and what it does, are to a worldly heart.”
“Why does medicine, if it does good, purge us and make us vomit?”
“To show that the Word, when it works effectively, cleanses the heart and mind. For look: what the one does to the body, the other does to the soul.”
“What should we learn from seeing the flame of our fire go upward, and from seeing the beams and sweet influence of the sun strike downward?”

“From the fire going up we are taught to rise toward heaven with fervent, burning desires. And from the sun sending its heat, its beams, and its sweet influence downward, we are taught that the Savior of the world, though he is high, reaches down to us below with his grace and love.”
“Where do the clouds get their water?”
“From the sea.”
“What may we learn from that?”
“That ministers should draw their teaching from God.”
“Why do they empty themselves on the earth?”
“To show that ministers should give out what they know of God to the world.”
“Why is the rainbow caused by the sun?”
“To show that the covenant of God’s grace is confirmed to us in Christ.”
“Why do the springs come to us from the sea, through the earth?”
“To show that the grace of God comes to us through the body of Christ.”
“Why do some springs rise from the tops of high hills?”
“To show that the spirit of grace will spring up in some who are great and mighty, as well as in many who are poor and lowly.”
“Why does the fire take hold of the candle’s wick?”
“To show that unless grace kindles in the heart, there will be no true light of life in us.”
“Why are the wick and the tallow and all of it used up to keep the candle burning?”
“To show that body and soul and everything should be at the service of the grace of God that is in us, and spend themselves to keep it in good condition.”
“Why does the pelican pierce her own breast with her beak?”
“To feed her young with her blood, and so to show that Christ the blessed so loves his young, his people, that he saves them from death by his blood.”
“What can one learn from hearing the rooster crow?”

“Learn to remember Peter’s sin, and Peter’s repentance. The rooster’s crowing also shows that day is coming on; so let the crowing of the rooster remind you of that last and terrible day of judgment.”
